ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: This study received ethical approval from the North West -Greater Manchester Central NHS Research Ethics Committee (23/NW/0163) and was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06054009).

All participants completed baseline, post-therapy, and one-month follow-up research assessments with a research assistant (MA or GS) who was not blind to allocation, but was independent from therapy delivery.
In the final assessment, participants were invited to give verbal and/or written qualitative feedback about the therapy and study procedures.

Participants were outpatients recruited from services for young people in Birmingham Women's and Children's NHS Foundation Trust (BWC) mental health services through clinician referral and self-referral via posters and leaflets displayed in BWC waiting rooms.

Four participants were recruited for Intervention 3, as planned. Since Kazdin, (2021) states that 'a minimal [sic] of two [baselines] is possible but infrequently used' (p.58), the data for Intervention 1 were retained despite under-recruiting.
table.formatted: Four participants were recruited for Intervention 3, as planned. <ref type="bibr">Since Kazdin, (2021)</ref> states that 'a minimal [sic] of two [baselines] is possible but infrequently used' (p.58), the data for Intervention 1 were retained despite under-recruiting.

table.text: At consent, participants gave permission for the research team to access their medical records to extract their recorded diagnosis and prescribed medication.
This was done by EČ whilst participants were enrolled in the study.
The demographic characteristics of participants are shown in Table 1.
table.formatted: The demographic characteristics of participants are shown in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>.

table.text: The majority (4 participants; 44%) were White, 2 (22%) Black, 2 (22%) mixed/multiple backgrounds, and 1 (11%) Asian. 8 of the 9 participants had previously received psychological therapy before, but only 1 had received therapy specifically for dissociation.
All other participants were prescribed an SSRI (escitalopram 20mg; fluoxetine 30-40mg; sertraline 25-100mg).
Additionally, two participants were prescribed antipsychotic medication (P1 and P4; aripiprazole 15mg and olanzapine 10mg); P4 was prescribed lamotrigine, and P5 melatonin.
Participants were invited to record the review in any way they would find helpful, including audio or video 'selfie' recordings.
Participants were supported to identify their positive beliefs facilitating worry as well as the negative effects of worry: this built the rationale for introducing the worry time technique.
If indicated, participants were encouraged to design a behavioural experiment to further challenge their beliefs.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Dissociation CBT Studies (DisCS).
table.research_questions:
The study is not powered for hypothesis testing, but has the following objectives:

Primary
	To determine whether the psychological intervention reduces the psychological maintenance mechanism (factor) of interest (i.e. cognitive appraisals [study 1]; perseverative thinking [study 2]; affect intolerance [study 3]).

Secondary
	To gain a preliminary indication of whether the relationship between the proposed psychological factor (cognitive appraisals; perseverative thinking; affect intolerance) and ‘felt sense of anomaly’-type dissociation is causal.

Tertiary/Qualitative
	To improve the therapy intervention for use in future treatment development studies.
table.study_type: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.q5: There will not be blinding, but to increase impartiality, the assessments will be undertaken by a research assistant (i.e., not by the therapist).
table.study_design_overview:
This project consists of three randomised multiple baseline design (MBD) single case experimental design studies, with an A1B1A2 structure (Appendix A).
Each study will have four participants. After completing a baseline assessment, each will be randomised to a different length of baseline (phase A1) duration (either 1, 2, 3 or 4 weeks). During A1, participants will rate the target maintenance mechanism (factor) and their level of dissociation daily (see Section 9.6, Assessments).
The treatment window (phase B1) for each participant in all studies will be five weeks. In this time, participants will have four 1:1 one-hour long psychological therapy sessions with a qualified clinical psychologist who will deliver the study intervention (see Section 10, Study Interventions). Between-session tasks will be set as part of this intervention, to be completed by the participant alone, or with telephone or additional in-person support from the research team. Participants will continue to rate the maintenance mechanism factor and their dissociation every other day. At the end of the intervention window (phase B1), participants will repeat the baseline assessment measures in a ‘post-intervention’ assessment.
The follow-up phase – phase A2 – will last for one month following the closure of the intervention window (phase B1). In this phase, participants will continue to make ratings of the maintenance mechanism factor and their dissociation every other day. At the end of phase A2, participants will complete the baseline assessment measures again in a ‘follow-up’ assessment, and will be offered the chance to provide unstructured qualitative feedback about the research processes and intervention. 64f0a4d0d9f2c90586d048ae DiSCS - Protocol v1.1 - 2023-07-10.pdf https://osf.io/project/8vezm/files/osfstorage/64f0a4d0d9f2c90586d048ae https://osf.io/download/64f0a4d0d9f2c90586d048ae 8b75b8cb6b2f8abd2b5e151a3a0be8ced7f40a21ad1953fedcad57a8e6e8645a
table.randomization: The baseline phase (A1) will be randomised: participants will wait either 1, 2, 3 or 4 weeks before beginning the intervention phase. This will be achieved via preparation of sealed envelopes by a researcher who is not involved in the study.

table.sample_size_rationale: The aim of SCED studies is to use repeated phases with and without the application of the experimental intervention to demonstrate that it is the intervention that is causing the observed effect. In essence, this allows the same participant to contribute both control and intervention data, increasing information about probable cause and effect in contexts where it may not be feasible to run a fully powered randomised controlled trial. General convention suggests that demonstrating changes in the outcome measure after introducing or withdrawing the intervention must be done a minimum of four times to imply a functional relationship between intervention and effect. Typically, this can be achieved by repeatedly introducing and withdrawing an intervention with the same participant. However, this method is less valid in clinical psychology, where carry-over effects are expected from the intervention, and repeating the intervention may not be practicable. Thus, the multiple-baseline design (MBD) across individuals allows the requisite number of transitions (from intervention to ‘no intervention’ and vice versa) to be achieved, whilst each participant only undergoes the treatment once. Randomising the length of the baseline phase for each participant means that any observed effect cannot be better understood as a function of time elapsed since the baseline assessment or other research procedure. The minimum number of participants required for an MBD study is two, although three or more is typical. Thus, this project will use a sample size of four participants per study, to mitigate against any potential drop out or high levels of missing data.
table.stopping_rule: There are no interim analyses or formal stopping rules in relation to this study given the small sample size and its exploratory nature.
table.manipulated_variables:
Study 1: Cognitive appraisals of dissociation.
Study 2: Perseverative thinking.
Study 3: Affect intolerance.
table.measured_variables: Visual analogue scales (0-100 ratings) for the manipulated variable and for FSA-dissociation.
table.statistical_tests:
Given the design and sample size, analysis will be descriptive in nature and no hypothesis testing will be carried out. The three studies will be analysed separately according to the following analysis plan.

1. Quantitative data
First, patient outcome measures will be presented graphically, and visual and statistical analysis used to assess within- and between-phase data patterns, as per the recommendations for SCEDs.

•	Within-phase analysis: 
o	level (mean and standard deviation and/or median and interquartile range); 
o	trend (visual analysis or whether datapoints are increasing / decreasing);
o	stability (whether 80-90% of datapoints fall within 15% of the mean or median40).

•	Between-phase analysis:
o	Immediacy of effect (visual analysis);
o	Consistency of data patterns (visual analysis; trend analysis);
o	Overlap between phases (nonoverlap statistics e.g. extended celeration line or two standard deviation band method; as appropriate).

The above information will be used to form a judgement as to whether the data indicates that the intervention is causing a change in outcome measure scores. If so, effect sizes (Tau-U) will be calculated.

2. Qualitative data
Written and transcribed qualitative data arising from requests for feedback on the research process and therapy intervention (see Protocol section 9.6.3, Qualitative Feedback) will be analysed using Thematic Analysis. This analysis will be managed within qualitative analysis software. Quality guidelines will be followed, including credibility checks and reflexive practice. This approach has been used before by the CI with a similar participant group6. Key themes arising from this analysis will be reported within the study results.
table.missing_data_handling: There will be no statistical methods applied for handling missing data as this approach is inconsistent with the single experimental case design. For each participant, phases with fewer than five datapoints will be omitted from analysis, since this is the minimum recommended for within-phase analyses.
table.additional_comments: This study is also being pre-registered on ClinicalTrials.gov

live_data_statements: All participants completed baseline, post-therapy, and one-month follow-up research assessments with a research assistant (MA or GS) who was not blind to allocation, but was independent from therapy delivery.
In the final assessment, participants were invited to give verbal and/or written qualitative feedback about the therapy and study procedures.

Participants were outpatients recruited from services for young people in Birmingham Women's and Children's NHS Foundation Trust (BWC) mental health services through clinician referral and self-referral via posters and leaflets displayed in BWC waiting rooms.

Four participants were recruited for Intervention 3, as planned. Since Kazdin, (2021) states that 'a minimal [sic] of two [baselines] is possible but infrequently used' (p.58), the data for Intervention 1 were retained despite under-recruiting.
At consent, participants gave permission for the research team to access their medical records to extract their recorded diagnosis and prescribed medication.
This was done by EČ whilst participants were enrolled in the study.
The demographic characteristics of participants are shown in Table 1.

The majority (4 participants; 44%) were White, 2 (22%) Black, 2 (22%) mixed/multiple backgrounds, and 1 (11%) Asian. 8 of the 9 participants had previously received psychological therapy before, but only 1 had received therapy specifically for dissociation.
All other participants were prescribed an SSRI (escitalopram 20mg; fluoxetine 30-40mg; sertraline 25-100mg).
Additionally, two participants were prescribed antipsychotic medication (P1 and P4; aripiprazole 15mg and olanzapine 10mg); P4 was prescribed lamotrigine, and P5 melatonin.
Participants were invited to record the review in any way they would find helpful, including audio or video 'selfie' recordings.
Participants were supported to identify their positive beliefs facilitating worry as well as the negative effects of worry: this built the rationale for introducing the worry time technique.
If indicated, participants were encouraged to design a behavioural experiment to further challenge their beliefs.

text.text: Dissociative experiences are common and transdiagnostic.
Yet causal evidence for psychological mechanisms of dissociation remains scarce, particularly in youth.

Our group has developed a translational cognitive-behavioural model of a subset of common dissociative experiences (FSA-dissociation), but causal relationships proposed within this model remain to be tested.
This study sought to experimentally test three causal relationships proposed in the FSAdissociation CBT model using an interventionist-causal paradigm.
A benefit of this method is the opportunity it provides to simultaneously develop targeted therapeutic techniques whilst empirically testing the underlying theory.

We conducted a randomised multiple baseline experimental design study with nine NHS patients (aged 16 to 23), targeting three hypothesised mechanisms of change: cognitive appraisals of dissociation, perseverative thinking, and affect intolerance.
The study was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06054009).
Each participant received four sessions of individual CBT with a clinical psychologist targeting one hypothesised mechanism.
Analysis indicated successful targeting of cognitive appraisals, and partial success for affect intolerance and perseverative thinking.
Findings tentatively support cognitive appraisals and affect intolerance as candidate causal mechanisms in youth dissociation.
Any effect of targeting perseverative thinking was better accounted for by reduced cognitive appraisals.
Although phase instability limited inference, this study offers novel causal insights into transdiagnostic dissociation and informs early-stage treatment development for this presentation.

Namely, it suggests that future psychological interventions for transdiagnostic dissociation in youth should incorporate targeting of cognitive appraisals, but that further research is required to determine whether affect intolerance constitutes a therapeutic target in this context.
Dissociation involves confusing and upsetting feelings of unreality, unfamiliarity, or disconnection in relation to your mind, body, or surroundings (Černis et al., 2020).

text.text: For example, some people describe being detached from their own emotions, including affection for loved ones, or feeling profoundly 'strange', as though they are living life from behind a thick pane of glass.
In children, adolescents, and young adults, such experiences are prevalent: more so than in later stages of life (Černis et al., 2023).

Transdiagnostic dissociative experiences are increasingly being implicated in the development and maintenance of other mental health problems, such as anxiety, depression, and psychosis (Černis, Evans, et al., 2021; Černis, Molodynski, et al., 2022; Černis, Antonović, et al., 2025).

text.formatted: We first identified a subtype of common dissociative experiences that are unified by a core phenomenological experience of a 'felt sense of anomaly' (FSA) <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Černis, Beierl, et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Černis et al., 2020)</ref>, thus also incorporating depersonalisation and derealisation experiences, such as feelings of unreality, disconnection, and unfamiliarity of one's body, perceptions, and internal and external world.

text.text: This subtype of dissociative experiences (FSA-dissociation) was then demonstrated to be common and transdiagnostic (Černis, Evans, et al., 2021; Černis, Molodynski, et al., 2022; Černis et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This subtype of dissociative experiences (FSA-dissociation) was then demonstrated to be common and transdiagnostic <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Černis, Evans, et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Černis, Molodynski, et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Černis et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Having defined the core problem to be addressed, we then identified plausible mechanisms underlying FSA-dissociation, resulting in a theoretical cognitive model of the problem (Černis, Ehlers, et al., 2022; Černis, Johns, et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Having defined the core problem to be addressed, we then identified plausible mechanisms underlying FSA-dissociation, resulting in a theoretical cognitive model of the problem <ref type="bibr">(Černis, Ehlers, et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Černis, Johns, et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Briefly, this model posits that FSAdissociation is interpreted as an internal threat and maintained by two mutually reinforcing feedback loops.

A 'foreground' loop of negative cognitive appraisals and counterproductive coping strategies (including rumination) directly sustains the experience, whilst a 'background' loop of affect intolerance and low subjective self-efficacy provides the context for the initial and continued threat interpretation.

Whilst some observational support has been found for aspects of this theoretical model in young people (Černis et al., 2026; Esteban Serna et al., in prep.), to proceed with the translational intervention development process, the model must now be experimentally validated.
text.formatted: Whilst some observational support has been found for aspects of this theoretical model in young people <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Černis et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Esteban Serna et al., in prep.)</ref>, to proceed with the translational intervention development process, the model must now be experimentally validated.

text.text: That is, evidence is required to support the proposed causal relationships between the mechanisms outlined in the model and FSA-dissociation.
Further, methods for targeting and ameliorating the mechanisms must be identified: if they are not amenable to psychological intervention, they cannot be targets in a model-driven therapy protocol.

The interventionist-causal paradigm (e.g., Kendler & Campbell, 2009) has proven useful in recent similar programmes of translational research (Freeman, Dunn, et al., 2015; Freeman, Waite, et al., 2015) as a method for pursuing both objectives simultaneously.
text.formatted: The interventionist-causal paradigm (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Kendler & Campbell, 2009)</ref> has proven useful in recent similar programmes of translational research <ref type="bibr">(Freeman, Dunn, et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Freeman, Waite, et al., 2015)</ref> as a method for pursuing both objectives simultaneously.

text.text: In this paradigm, a therapeutic technique is used to selectively manipulate (ameliorate) a mechanism and determine its indirect 'downstream' effect on the problem of interest (i.e., in the present context, determining whether dissociation subsequently also improves).

This method therefore requires two checks: first, that the manipulation (intervention) had an effect on the targeted mechanism; and second, whether that successful manipulation has any indirect effect on the clinical outcome.
At this early stage of the translational process, it is prudent to establish 'proof of concept' prior to larger-scale testing.

For this purpose, single case experimental designs (SCEDs) are a valuable methodological choice (Krasny-Pacini & Evans, 2018), since with careful design such studies have high internal validity, enabling evaluation of causality despite small sample sizes (Lobo et al., 2017).

text.text: SCED studies, or 'single-case experiments' (Morley, 2018), measure dependent variables repeatedly across phases where the intervention is delivered or withheld: effectively allowing each participant to act as their own control arm (Lobo et al., 2017).

text.text: Multiple baseline designs are a form of SCED that retain these benefits and may be more appropriate in psychological intervention research where it is more practicable to demonstrate replication of effects across multiple participants, rather than through repeated application and withdrawal of the intervention.

The aim of this study, therefore, is to test via multiple baseline design (MBD) methodology the three largest psychological contributors to FSA-dissociation as identified in previous cross-sectional research.
For Intervention 1, the mechanism of interest was negative cognitive appraisals of the dissociative experiences.

In network analyses of observational data, this proposed mechanism demonstrated a causal effect of 0.73 in a non-clinical adult group (Černis, Ehlers, et al., 2022) and 0.72 in a psychosis group (Černis, Molodynski, et al., 2022).

text.text: In order to determine the success of each intervention in modifying its intended target, the primary outcomes in this study were measures of these three psychological factors.
The secondary outcome was FSA-dissociation.
Where an intervention was successful, subsequent reductions in transdiagnostic dissociation may indicate preliminary experimental support for the proposed causal role of the targeted mechanism.
Such evidence is required to validate the theoretical model and refine treatment development efforts.
Successful interventions that reduce FSA-dissociation would be candidates for inclusion in a future targeted multi-modular intervention for transdiagnostic dissociation.

As such, the current study constitutes a 'proof of concept' study adopting an interventionist-causal paradigm to simultaneously test the theoretical model and inform early-stage treatment development.

The study used a randomised multiple baseline experimental design, with an 'AB + Follow-Up' structure (i.e., baseline phase, intervention phase, follow-up phase with no active intervention or therapist contact).

All participants completed baseline, post-therapy, and one-month follow-up research assessments with a research assistant (MA or GS) who was not blind to allocation, but was independent from therapy delivery.
In the final assessment, participants were invited to give verbal and/or written qualitative feedback about the therapy and study procedures.
For the baseline phase, each participant was randomly allocated to wait either one, two, three, or four weeks between the baseline assessment and the start of the intervention.
Randomisation of the baseline length is a design feature recommended to improve the scientific credibility of the study (Kazdin, 2019; Kratochwill et al., 2022).

text.text: Randomisation was carried out via the opening of a sealed envelope by the research assistant once all baseline measures had been fully completed.
Envelopes were prepared by a colleague who was not involved in the study.
The intervention phase was five weeks.
In this time, participants received four 1:1 one-hour long psychological therapy sessions with a qualified clinical psychologist (EČ) (see Intervention, below).
The follow-up phase was one month.
In this phase, there was no further contact with the therapist.

text.text: Participants were outpatients recruited from services for young people in Birmingham Women's and Children's NHS Foundation Trust (BWC) mental health services through clinician referral and self-referral via posters and leaflets displayed in BWC waiting rooms.
Additionally, we circulated study information to the research interest email list of the University of Birmingham Centre for Human Brain Health.

Inclusion criteria were: aged 16 years or over; experiencing significant levels of 'felt sense of anomaly'-type dissociation defined as a score within the 'moderate severe' or 'severe' range on the ČEFSA-14 (i.e., score of 39 or above) (Černis et al., 2023).

text.text: Exclusion criteria were: confirmed diagnosis of an Axis II ("personality") disorder; primary diagnosis of alcohol/substance dependency, organic syndrome, or learning disability; presence of risk issues that would be a clinical priority above managing dissociative symptoms (e.g., severe self-harm; active suicidal behaviour; etc.); and current engagement in any other individual psychological therapy (or psychological therapy due to begin within the participation window for this study).
We aimed to recruit 4 participants to each of the three interventions, and for participants receiving the same intervention to be recruited soon after one another.
This target was set since Kazdin, (2021) describes three or more baselines as typical for a multiple-baseline design.

For Intervention 1, one person declined to participate on the day of the scheduled (concurrent) baseline, and another was admitted to inpatient care shortly beforehand, resulting in only two participants for this intervention.
As a result, the methodology was amended to non-concurrent baselines for the following interventions.
Recruitment for Intervention 2 was closed at three participants due to recruitment delays.

Four participants were recruited for Intervention 3, as planned. Since Kazdin, (2021) states that 'a minimal [sic] of two [baselines] is possible but infrequently used' (p.58), the data for Intervention 1 were retained despite under-recruiting.

text.text: Two kinds of measures were employed in this study: 'standard' measures, which were selfreport validated psychometric measures completed at each of the three assessments -each measuring an element of the FSA-model -and 'target' measures (Morley, 2018).

text.text: Target measures were two visual analogue scales (VAS) completed daily (in baseline phase), or every other day (in intervention and follow-up phases).
The frequency was reduced in the latter two phases to reduce participant burden and support participant retention.

Target measures asked participants to rate from 0 to 100: 1) how much they have been bothered by the intervention-specific psychological factor (i.e., cognitive appraisals, perseverative thinking, or affect intolerance) since the last rating, and 2) the severity of the distress caused by their dissociative experiences since the last rating.
Measures were completed on hardcopy forms, or sent via text or email to the research assistant, according to participant preference.

In addition to the standard measures described below, at each assessment point, participants answered one item asking the frequency of recent self-harming behaviours ('In the past two weeks, how often have you deliberately self-harmed (e.g. cutting, burning, etc.) without intending to die?'), with a Likert scale rating from 0 (never) to 4 (daily or almost daily).
At baseline only, participants also completed demographics questions and questions regarding their previous receipt of psychological therapy.
At consent, participants gave permission for the research team to access their medical records to extract their recorded diagnosis and prescribed medication.
This was done by EČ whilst participants were enrolled in the study.
The ČEFSA-14 measures FSA-dissociation over the past two weeks on a Likert scale from 0 (never) to 4 (always).
Higher scores indicate more frequent FSA-dissociation, with an indicative scoring guide available for interpretation.

This scale has excellent psychometric properties (Cronbach's alpha=0.92), and demonstrates measure invariance across gender, clinical status, and age (from 13 to approximately 65 years) (Černis et al., 2023). text.text: Participants received four one-hour sessions of individual therapy with a qualified clinical psychologist with expertise in dissociative difficulties (EČ).
Sessions took place in-person at the University of Birmingham or the participant's home, according to their preference.
Therapy was provided in addition to usual care.
Procedural fidelity was not independently assessed.

In each intervention, the first session included socialisation to the therapy session format, and psychoeducation and formulation to describe how the targeted mechanism relates to the participant's dissociative experiences.

Sessions 1 to 3 included learning and practicing a targeted active change technique, and the final session focused on consolidation of new information and planning for the participant to continue therapeutic change independently.
The key change techniques were: cognitive restructuring (e.g., Beck, 2021) (Intervention 1), and worry postponement (e.g., Wells, 1999) (Intervention 2).
For Intervention 3, following psychoeducation (emotion literacy), Socratic dialogue was used to identify and challenge negative beliefs about emotions.

Motivational interviewing was then used to explore participants' readiness to change their relationship with their emotions, and tailored suggestions of relevant DBT skills were offered where appropriate, alongside supported practice to incrementally approach emotions.
Fuller description and justification of the interventions is included in Supplementary Materials.

For each intervention, standard and target measure data were analysed to determine whether the mechanism of interest (i.e., cognitive appraisals, perseverative thinking, affect intolerance) was effectively targeted by the intervention.
Indication of significant reduction in the intended mechanism was taken as a successful manipulation of the mechanism.
Next, for participants where the intervention successfully manipulated the targeted mechanism, standard and target measure data for dissociation were analysed.

Given our interest in causal mechanisms of dissociation, the remainder of the standard measure data was subject to exploratory analysis and used to inform interpretation of the results (see Supplementary Material).
To determine whether changes in standard measure scores were meaningful, data were analysed using the Jacobson and Truax method for evaluating reliable change (Morley & Dowzer, 2014).

text.text: Reliable change thresholds for each scale were calculated using reliability coefficients and standard deviations from peer-reviewed published studies (see Supplementary Material).
Changes were considered reliable where they exceeded 1.96 (corresponding to the 95% confidence interval of the standard normal distribution) times the standard error of difference for the scale.
Clinically significant change could not be calculated, as none of the scales had established clinical cut-offs or normative comparison data.

text.text: The mean age of participants was 19.8 years.

The majority (4 participants; 44%) were White, 2 (22%) Black, 2 (22%) mixed/multiple backgrounds, and 1 (11%) Asian. 8 of the 9 participants had previously received psychological therapy before, but only 1 had received therapy specifically for dissociation.
The mean ČEFSA score at baseline was 44.2 (SD=6.6), which is in the 'moderately severe' range.
Only one participant was not prescribed any psychiatric medication (P6).
All other participants were prescribed an SSRI (escitalopram 20mg; fluoxetine 30-40mg; sertraline 25-100mg).
Additionally, two participants were prescribed antipsychotic medication (P1 and P4; aripiprazole 15mg and olanzapine 10mg); P4 was prescribed lamotrigine, and P5 melatonin.

Whilst visual analysis of P6's data was hampered by very low stability, this pattern was clearer in P9's data.

Tau-U analysis supports this interpretation of P9's scores (only), with a significant maximum improvement both between baseline and intervention (Tau-U= -1, 90% CI= -1 --0.429, p=0.0039), and between baseline and follow-up phases (Tau-U= -1, 90% CI= -1 --0.452, p=0.0027).
We therefore considered the manipulation of affect intolerance successful for P9 only.

Since the visual and Tau-U analysis indicated a significant worsening in the targeted mechanism for P8, this was considered a significant manipulation of the targeted mechanism (in the opposite manner to that intended), and P8 was therefore included in analysis of the secondary objective to nevertheless evaluate the causal relationship between mechanism and dissociation.

The aim of this study was to test the proposed theoretical model of transdiagnostic dissociation whilst simultaneously identifying effective therapeutic techniques to be incorporated into a targeted intervention in future.
To the best of the authors' knowledge, this is the first study in the field of dissociation to address this particular translational objective.
Given the mixed results across the interventions, our results indicate both a need and direction for further treatment development.

The first intervention indicated that it is possible to target negative cognitive appraisals of transdiagnostic dissociation and that doing so is associated with reduced dissociative symptoms and distress about these, consistent with a causal relationship.
It is striking that with only four sessions, both participants' dissociation scores reduced below the study entry criterion.

Such efficacy is perhaps unsurprising, given that this technique is a core component of CBT interventions across the spectrum of mental health presentations, including within CBT for Depersonalisation-Derealisation Disorder (CBT-f-DDD) (Hunter et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Such efficacy is perhaps unsurprising, given that this technique is a core component of CBT interventions across the spectrum of mental health presentations, including within CBT for Depersonalisation-Derealisation Disorder (CBT-f-DDD) <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Hunter et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Evidence for targeting perseverative negative thinking in this context was mixed, however.
A plausible interpretation of the results from the second intervention is that any causal effect of rumination on dissociation is better accounted for by cognitive appraisals.
Reliable change in perseverative thinking was always accompanied by reliable change in cognitive appraisals, and any reductions in dissociation scores were seen concurrently or following those.

More work is required, therefore, to determine whether focusing on the process of rumination in a targeted intervention for transdiagnostic dissociation offers any additional benefits above and beyond addressing the content of negative cognitive appraisals.
Clients may find the worry management strategy helpful if they regularly become entrenched in their negative cognitive appraisals.
However, on the basis of this study, there is insufficient evidence to recommend that an intervention tailored to transdiagnostic dissociation should target the process of rumination specifically.

The proposal that affect intolerance maintains dissociative experiences is a distinct feature of our theoretical model compared to the CBT model for Depersonalisation-Derealisation Disorder (Hunter et al., 2003).
text.formatted: The proposal that affect intolerance maintains dissociative experiences is a distinct feature of our theoretical model compared to the CBT model for Depersonalisation-Derealisation Disorder <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Hunter et al., 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Though, notably, Vancappel and El-Hage's (2023) model of dissociation, proposed on the basis of existing literature, includes a similar mechanism in the form of negative beliefs about emotion.
In the third intervention, the manipulation of this target mechanism was not reliable, and as a result, it is not possible to make firm conclusions about causality.

Where some evidence of successful manipulation was present (i.e., for P9), there was mixed evidence for causality: visual analysis suggested a reduction, but this did not reach significance thresholds.

Further, the increased subjective distress related to affect (in)tolerance reported by P8 ("How much my relationship with my emotions has bothered me") demonstrates the need to refine the affect intolerance intervention delivered here in order to appropriately and ethically manage intervention-related symptom fluctuations, and mitigate against iatrogenic harm.

Qualitative feedback from participants provides an explanation for the mixed effects of the affect intolerance intervention: all participants highlighted the number of sessions (four) as insufficient.

This was perhaps particularly limiting when targeting affect intolerance, as it is likely that graded and repeated experiential work is required to produce meaningful change (Pascual-Leone & Greenberg, 2007).
text.formatted: This was perhaps particularly limiting when targeting affect intolerance, as it is likely that graded and repeated experiential work is required to produce meaningful change <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Pascual-Leone & Greenberg, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, a third recommendation for future treatment development work is to re-test the affect intolerance intervention using an increased number of sessions.

On the basis of this study, it is still too early to draw conclusions about whether affect intolerance is a psychological target amenable to modification in this group, and whether doing so would successfully reduce FSA-dissociation.

It is important to note that confidence in the conclusions from this study are limited by the low levels of within-phase stability within the majority of participants' data, and high between-participant heterogeneity.

Lack of stability reduces internal validity and makes it difficult to determine whether the intervention has truly produced a change in scores. Lobo et al., (2017, p. 3) state that 'it is recommended' that stability is established in the data before the intervention is introduced.

text.text: However, this is challenging to operationalise where the study design incorporates a randomised length of baseline in a multiple baseline design, and where practical considerations for booking therapy session appointments may reduce participant and research team ability to respond dynamically to 'live' phase-stability data.
Nevertheless, future research testing the hypotheses generated here should seek to address these challenges wherever possible.
No formal therapist competency or fidelity checks were conducted in the current study.
This project was an unfunded pilot study delivered by an experienced clinical psychologist with established training and routine practice in CBT with dissociation and young people.
Interventions were brief, manual-guided, and targeted at specific mechanisms, using established therapeutic techniques, which helped standardise delivery.
However, the absence of independent fidelity or competency assessment is acknowledged as a limitation and should be addressed in future, funded work.

This study therefore represents a preliminary, but critical, first step in the empirical testing of our theoretical model of FSA-dissociation, and the development of a translational targeted psychological intervention.
The findings are consistent with the proposed model, and tentatively support the use of CBT strategies addressing negative cognitive appraisals in the treatment of FSA-dissociation.
They also emphasise the need for further exploration of affect intolerance as a potentially amenable therapeutic target in this context.
Consideration of data stability and heterogeneity, therapy fidelity, and intervention 'dose' will ensure greater confidence in the validity of the findings.

In each intervention, the first session included socialisation to the therapy session format, and psychoeducation and formulation to describe how the targeted mechanism relates to the participant's dissociative experiences.

Sessions 1 to 3 included learning and practicing a targeted active change technique (see below), and the final session focused on consolidation of new information and planning for the participant to continue therapeutic change independently.

Following advice from lived experience advisors consulted during the design of this study, each session ended with a 'review and recap' to support participants to remember the session despite potential dissociation-related memory difficulties.
The review questions prompted participants to identify a key learning point and to explicitly plan how to remember this between sessions.
Participants were invited to record the review in any way they would find helpful, including audio or video 'selfie' recordings.
The key therapeutic technique delivered was cognitive restructuring, drawn from classical cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT; e.g., Beck, 2021).
text.formatted: The key therapeutic technique delivered was cognitive restructuring, drawn from classical cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT; e.g., <ref type="bibr">Beck, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The aim was for participants to become aware of the automatic appraisals they make of their dissociative experiences and replace catastrophic interpretations with more balanced judgements.
The key technique in this intervention was the restriction and management of worry via the use of 'worry time'.
Participants were supported to identify their positive beliefs facilitating worry as well as the negative effects of worry: this built the rationale for introducing the worry time technique.
In contrast to Intervention 1, the content of the worrying thoughts was not addressed or reappraised.

This technique has been thoroughly tested in interventionist-causal paradigms in the context of psychosis (Foster et al., 2010; Freeman et al., 2015 Freeman et al., , 2021)), where it has been demonstrated to be effective in reducing worry, and thus, paranoia.
text.formatted: This technique has been thoroughly tested in interventionist-causal paradigms in the context of psychosis <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Foster et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Freeman et al., 2015</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Freeman et al., , 2021))</ref>, where it has been demonstrated to be effective in reducing worry, and thus, paranoia.

text.text: It was therefore anticipated to have a similar effect in the context of FSA-dissociation.
This intervention incorporated psychoeducation about emotions (emotion literacy) and identification of participants' own beliefs about emotions.

The latter was facilitated by using selected items from the AIS (Stapinski et al., 2014) and common 'emotion myths' (Leahy et al., 2011, p.232; e.g., 'being emotional means being out of control') as starting points for discussion in session 1.
text.formatted: The latter was facilitated by using selected items from the AIS <ref type="bibr">(Stapinski et al., 2014)</ref> and common 'emotion myths' <ref type="bibr">(Leahy et al., 2011, p.232</ref>; e.g., 'being emotional means being out of control') as starting points for discussion in session 1.

text.text: In session 2, participants' beliefs about emotion were further explored via Socratic dialogue with a CBT cognitive restructuring worksheet providing scaffolding for this discussion.
If indicated, participants were encouraged to design a behavioural experiment to further challenge their beliefs.
Session 3 used a motivational interviewing framework to explore participants' readiness to change their relationship with their emotions.

If indicated, they were then introduced to selected dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) techniques and concepts, alongside supported practice to incrementally approach emotions (e.g., purposefully engaging fully with a sad song, with a plan for how to emotionally repair afterwards).
This discussion was tailored to participants: thus, no participant engaged in every strategy.

Intervention 1: exploratory findings Exploratory analysis of the other standard measures indicated that there were also changes from baseline for both participants in PTQ scores (P1: post-therapy and follow-up; P2: follow-up only).
Additionally, P1 showed changes in GSE at post-therapy and follow-up, and P2 showed improvements on AIS at follow-up.
